svg.aria-label: Diagram: how Elastic Beanstalk Cluster Mode changes the unit of infrastructure. On the left, Standard Mode, the model Beanstalk has always used: each application gets a dedicated environment with its own load balancer, its own instances and its own idle headroom, so forty small services mean forty sets of spare capacity that cannot be shared. A note records the structural ceiling: the default Elastic Beanstalk quota is 200 environments per account per Region, and that limit applies across applications rather than per application, so a fleet running production and staging for each service consumes two environments per application against that shared total, while the applications quota itself is 75 per account per Region. On the right, Cluster Mode: multiple applications run on pooled infrastructure powered by Amazon EKS instead of a dedicated environment per application, so headroom is shared across the pool and the density ceiling is no longer set by the environment count. The managed feature set is listed: event-driven autoscaling, OpenTelemetry observability to CloudWatch and third-party providers, Secrets Manager integration and HTTPS by default through Certificate Manager. A panel at the bottom records where the economics turn: there is no additional charge for Cluster Mode itself, but you pay for the EKS cluster and EKS Auto Mode charges, which is a fixed cost the per-application model did not carry, and AWS states the saving arrives as your applications scale or your application count grows rather than universally.
svg.title: The unit of infrastructure moves from the application to the pool
svg.text: Beanstalk was always the silo model with the details hidden
Cluster Mode keeps the hiding and changes the model underneath.
Standard Mode — one environment per application
app A
own LB, own
instances, own idle
app B
own LB, own
instances, own idle
app C
own LB, own
instances, own idle
Excellent blast-radius isolation. Poor density — forty
small services means forty sets of idle headroom that
cannot be lent to each other.
The ceiling is the environment count, not the app count:
200 environments / account / Region
“applies across applications, not per application” · apps quota: 75
Cluster Mode — pooled infrastructure, on EKS
app A · app B · app C · …
one pool, shared headroom, powered by Amazon EKS
“instead of a dedicated environment per application”
Density improves with count. Isolation degrades with it.
What comes with it
• event-driven autoscaling
• OpenTelemetry → CloudWatch and third parties
• Secrets Manager integration
• HTTPS by default via Certificate Manager
Where the economics turn — both halves are in one sentence
“There is no additional charge for Cluster Mode. You pay for the AWS resources your applications consume,
including the EKS cluster and EKS Auto Mode charges.”
A standing cost the per-application model never had — which is why the saving is stated as arriving “as your application count grows.”
Below the crossover, a pool costs more than the environments it replaces. Two or three services are the wrong shape for this; forty are the right one.
The modes coexist. Draw the pool around a blast radius somebody chose — by ownership and release cadence, not by what is cheapest on paper.
